diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_MISSING_OUTPUT
diagnostics.message: no output file given; use -o FILE or --output FILE
diagnostics.cause: The output file name is a mandatory parameter, so that the compiler never guesses where to put the generated binary and never overwrites a file the caller did not name.  Add -o followed by the path of the executable to create.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_NO_INPUT
diagnostics.message: no input files given
diagnostics.cause: At least one source file must be named on the command line.  This usually means the file list was produced by a shell glob that matched nothing, or that every argument was consumed as the value of an option.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_BAD_SUFFIX
diagnostics.message: input file '{path}' does not have the '.pl4g' suffix
diagnostics.cause: Source files are recognized by their '.pl4g' suffix.  A file with any other suffix is rejected rather than guessed at, because silently treating an unrelated file as source would produce a cascade of confusing syntax errors.  Rename the file, or check whether an option value was mistaken for a positional argument.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_UNKNOWN_OPTION
diagnostics.message: unrecognized command line option '{option}'
diagnostics.cause: The option is not known to this compiler.  Both compiler implementations accept the same options, so an option that works with one and not the other is a defect worth reporting.  Use --help to list the accepted options.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_DUPLICATE_OUTPUT
diagnostics.message: output file specified more than once; previously '{previous}'
diagnostics.cause: Exactly one output file may be named.  Repeating -o is rejected rather than resolved by taking the last one, because a generated command line that accumulates an extra -o is far more likely to be a defect in the generator than a deliberate override.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_NOT_IMPLEMENTED
diagnostics.message: option '{option}' is accepted by this compiler but not yet implemented
diagnostics.cause: The bootstrap compiler accepts the full option set of the final compiler so that build systems need not distinguish between them, but it does not implement every option yet.  This is a limitation of the bootstrap compiler, not an error in the command line.

spec.requirement: The Python implementation will accept the same parameters as the actual, full compiler.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_MISSING_ARGUMENT
diagnostics.message: option '{option}' requires an argument
diagnostics.cause: The option takes a value which was not supplied, usually because it was the last word of the command line or because the following word began with a dash and was taken as a separate option.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_BAD_ARGUMENT
diagnostics.message: invalid argument '{value}' for option '{option}'; expected one of {expected}
diagnostics.cause: The option accepts only a fixed set of values.  Check the spelling of the value against the list in the message or in --help.

spec.requirement: Initially, the compiler will require a parameter `-o` or `--output` with a mandatory argument to specify the output file name (just like existing compilers like gcc).  Additional parameters are the names of the source files, ending with the extension `.pl4g`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_UNKNOWN_TARGET
diagnostics.message: unknown target '{triple}'
diagnostics.cause: No backend is registered for this target triple.  The bootstrap compiler supports a subset of the targets the final compiler will support; the supported ones are listed by --help.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_UNKNOWN_WARNING
diagnostics.message: unknown warning name '{name}' in '{option}'
diagnostics.cause: The name given to -W or -Wno- does not match any controllable diagnostic.  The controllable names are the 'option' fields of the shared diagnostic catalog; note that errors cannot be disabled.

spec.requirement: Errors and warnings the compiler emits can be handled in the code.  To enable this, errors and warnings must be unique, constant, and consistent numbers.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_UNKNOWN_MCLEVEL
diagnostics.message: '{level}' is not something '{triple}' can be built for; {detail}

args.name: detail
args.description: what the target says is wrong with it

diagnostics.cause: What may be asked for is each architecture's own business.  x86-64 has four levels, which are the names its own documentation gives to what a processor of a given age can do, so a name is one of four.  RISC-V has no such list: its base is small and everything else is an extension, so what may be asked for is a string naming them -- `rv64gc` -- or a profile, which is a published set of them under one name -- `rva23`.  A name from one architecture means nothing to another.

spec.requirement: '--mclevel' names something the target can be built for.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_CLI_NO_MCLEVELS
diagnostics.message: '{triple}' has no microarchitecture levels
diagnostics.cause: An architecture has levels where its own documentation defines them, which x86-64 does and the others this compiler generates for do not.  Asking for one where there are none is asking for something with no meaning, rather than asking for the only thing there is.

spec.requirement: '--mclevel' is given only for a target that has levels.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_INPUT_UNREADABLE
diagnostics.message: cannot read '{path}': {reason}
diagnostics.cause: The source file could not be opened or read.  Common causes are a mistyped path, a file that was removed between the glob and the compilation, or insufficient permissions.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_OUTPUT_UNWRITABLE
diagnostics.message: cannot write '{path}': {reason}
diagnostics.cause: The output file could not be created or written.  Common causes are a non-existent directory, insufficient permissions, or a full file system.  The compiler writes the output only after code generation has succeeded, so a failure here leaves any previous output untouched.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_INVALID_UTF8
diagnostics.message: source file is not valid UTF-8 (at byte offset {offset})

args.name: offset
args.description: byte offset of the first invalid sequence

diagnostics.cause: Source text must be encoded in UTF-8.  A file saved in a single-byte encoding such as ISO-8859-1 will fail here as soon as it contains a non-ASCII character.  Re-encode the file as UTF-8.

spec.requirement: The compiler and well as any generated program requires that the encoding of text uses UTF-8 encoding.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_UNEXPECTED_CHAR
diagnostics.message: unexpected character {char} in source

args.name: char
args.description: the character and its code point

diagnostics.cause: The character cannot begin any token.  Since the language uses Unicode glyphs for several operators, this is often a glyph that resembles the intended one without being it, such as a hyphen-minus where a dash was meant, or a full-width character pasted from another document.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_UNTERMINATED_STRING
diagnostics.message: unterminated string literal
diagnostics.cause: A string literal was not closed before the end of the line.  String literals do not span lines; a closing quotation mark may be missing, or a backslash immediately before it may have escaped it unintentionally.

spec.requirement: Strings are written as in C/C++ and many other languages enclosed in `"` and supporting an escape notation like modern C and C++ for special characters as well as the Unicode notation.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_BAD_ESCAPE
diagnostics.message: unknown escape sequence '\\{char}' in string literal
diagnostics.cause: The character following the backslash does not form a recognized escape sequence.  The recognized escapes follow modern C and C++, including the \\u and \\U Unicode notations.  A literal backslash must be written as two backslashes.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_ASCII_SUBSTITUTE
diagnostics.message: '{ascii}' is accepted as a substitute for '{glyph}'
diagnostics.cause: The language is meant to be generated rather than typed, so the Unicode glyph is the canonical spelling and is what the compiler itself emits.  Multi-character ASCII substitutes are accepted for convenience while editing by hand; single characters are never substitutes, so that they remain available for future language features.  The substitution is reported only when this warning is asked for, since it is accepted usage rather than a defect.

spec.requirement: It is not important that keyboard support for entering the language exists which opens the door to using Unicode glyphs for operators and functions.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_INTEGER_RANGE
diagnostics.message: integer literal {literal} does not fit in type '{type}'
diagnostics.cause: The value of the literal lies outside the range the type can represent.  Because the language admits no undefined behaviour and no surprising interpretation of inputs, an out-of-range literal is an error rather than a silent truncation or wrap-around.

spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_BAD_LITERAL_SUFFIX
diagnostics.message: '{suffix}' is not an integer type, so it cannot be the suffix of a literal
diagnostics.cause: The suffix of an integer literal is the name of the integer type the literal has: one of i8, i16, i32, i64, u8, u16, u32 and u64.  Any other name, including the name of a type that is not an integer, has no meaning there.

spec.requirement: An integer literal states its type with a suffix naming that type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_LONELY_NEGATIVE
diagnostics.message: the sign of a negative literal must be followed immediately by digits
diagnostics.cause: A leading superscript minus is part of how a number is written, not an operator applied to one, so nothing may stand between it and the digits -- no space, and no other expression.  Writing it apart from the digits would make it a second spelling of subtraction, which is what having a separate glyph for the sign avoids.

spec.requirement: A negative literal is written with a leading superscript minus and no space: nothing stands between the sign and the digits.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_UNTERMINATED_CHARACTER
diagnostics.message: character literal is not closed before the end of the line
diagnostics.cause: A character literal is one code point between apostrophes and neither of them may be left out.  A literal that runs to the end of the line is usually an apostrophe written for something else -- an English possessive in a comment that is not a comment, or a quotation mark of the wrong kind.

spec.requirement: A character literal is closed with an apostrophe on the line it began on.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_CHARACTER_IS_ONE
diagnostics.message: a character literal holds one code point, and {found} were written

args.name: found
args.description: how many code points were written between the apostrophes

diagnostics.cause: A value of 'char' is one code point, so a literal of one is written with exactly one between the apostrophes.  Several of them are a string, which is written between quotation marks; none of them is nothing, which is not a value of any type.  A code point that takes several characters to type is written with an escape, which counts as the one it denotes.

spec.requirement: A character literal holds exactly one code point.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_INCONSISTENT_INDENT
diagnostics.message: indentation does not match any enclosing block
diagnostics.cause: A line is indented less than the current block but more than the block that encloses it, so it belongs to neither.  This usually results from mixing tab and space indentation, or from a generator that computed an indentation width inconsistently.

spec.requirement: Layout-based syntax uses rules and syntax similar to Python.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_MIXED_BLOCK_STYLE
diagnostics.message: layout and explicit '{{' '}}' block syntax cannot be mixed within one block
diagnostics.cause: A single block uses one notation throughout: either indentation, or braces with semicolon-separated statements.  Nested blocks may each choose their own notation, but a block may not change notation part way through.

spec.requirement: Indentation and explicit syntax cannot be mixed for individual blocks but properly nested blocks can have different syntaxes.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_TAB_INDENT
diagnostics.message: tab character used for indentation
diagnostics.cause: Indentation is measured in characters, so a tab would make the layout depend on a tab width that is not part of the language.  Because the language admits no surprising interpretation of inputs, tabs are rejected in indentation rather than assigned an arbitrary width.

spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_UNEXPECTED_TOKEN
diagnostics.message: expected {expected}, found {found}
diagnostics.cause: The parser reached a token that cannot continue the construct being parsed.  The message names what would have been accepted at that point.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_EXPECTED_BLOCK
diagnostics.message: expected ':' or '{{' to begin the function body
diagnostics.cause: A function header is followed either by a colon and an indented block, or by a brace-enclosed block of semicolon-separated statements.  A header with neither has no body.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: In layout format, the function header is followed by a colon, a newline, and then the properly indented code.  When the function header is followed by a `{` it uses the explicit syntax and continues until the respective closing `}`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FILESTRUCT_UNEXPECTED_TOPLEVEL
diagnostics.message: {construct} is not allowed at the top level of a file
diagnostics.cause: Only module handling, compile-time assertions and contracts, type definitions, variable definitions and function definitions may appear at the top level.  Statements that execute at run time belong inside a function; use a constructor function if the intent was to run code before the startup function.

spec.requirement: At the top level of a file one can find: module handling, compile-time expressions as assertions and contracts, type definitions, variable definitions, function definitions

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_DUPLICATE_PARAMETER
diagnostics.message: parameter '{name}' is declared more than once
diagnostics.cause: Each parameter of a function must have a distinct name, since otherwise a reference to that name in the body would be ambiguous.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: fn NAME(ARG1: TYPE1, [ARGN: TYPEN]) → RETVALTYPE BLOCK

diagnostics.name: LANG_VARDEF_EXPECTED_COLON
diagnostics.message: expected ':' after the name of the variable
diagnostics.cause: A variable definition always carries a colon, whether or not the type is written after it: `let x: u8 = 3u8` states the type, and `let x := 3u8` leaves it to be taken from the value.  The colon is what marks the construct as a definition.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Variable Definition
spec.requirement: A variable is defined with `let NAME: TYPE = VALUE`.  The type may be left out, in which case it is the type of the value.  There is no definition without a value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_VARDEF_MISSING_INITIALIZER
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is defined without a value
diagnostics.cause: A variable is given its value where it is defined; there is no form that leaves one uninitialized.  A variable that had no value would have to hold something the program never named, which is exactly the kind of unstated meaning this language does not admit -- and no rule about what that something is would make it stated.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Variable Definition
spec.requirement: A variable is defined with `let NAME: TYPE = VALUE`.  The type may be left out, in which case it is the type of the value.  There is no definition without a value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_CLOSING_PAREN
diagnostics.message: expected ')' to close the group
diagnostics.cause: Parentheses in an expression say which operator applies to what, so one that is opened has to be closed.  Check for a missing operand or an operator written where an operand was wanted.

spec.requirement: An expression may be enclosed in parentheses, which say how its operators group and mean nothing else.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_MEMBER
diagnostics.message: expected the name of something after '.'
diagnostics.cause: A dot names something through the thing it belongs to, so a name has to follow it.  Nothing else may.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, and what it holds is named through it as `NAME.thing`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_IMPORT_EXPECTED_NAME
diagnostics.message: expected the name of a module, written as a string
diagnostics.cause: What `import` is given is the name of a module, written in quotes.  It is not an expression and is not computed: the module is found and read while the program is being compiled, so the name has to be there to read.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, and what it holds is named through it as `NAME.thing`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_IMPORT_QUALIFIED
diagnostics.message: '{name}' names a module, which cannot be given a type or made mutable

args.name: name
args.description: the name the module is bound to

diagnostics.cause: A module is not a value.  Nothing can be computed from one, nothing of it survives into the program but the definitions it holds, and there is accordingly nothing to give a type to and nothing to change.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, and what it holds is named through it as `NAME.thing`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_IMPORT_INSIDE_FUNCTION
diagnostics.message: '{name}' imports a module inside a function, where a module cannot go

args.name: name
args.description: the name the module was to be bound to

diagnostics.cause: A module is read while the program is being compiled and what it holds belongs to the program, not to one function that happens to run.  An import therefore stands at the top level of a file, where the things it brings in are things the file has.

spec.requirement: A module is brought into a file with `let NAME := import("somename")`, at the top level of that file.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_NOT_ASSOCIATIVE
diagnostics.message: '{first}' and '{second}' cannot be written one after the other
diagnostics.cause: Some operators join two things and no more, because a third would have two readings and neither is what anyone means.  A comparison answers with a truth value, so `a < b < c` would compare that answer with a number.  ⊼ and ⊽ are not associative at all: `a ⊼ b ⊼ c` is one thing grouped to the left and a different thing grouped to the right.  Where one of those really was meant, parentheses say which; where a value was meant to lie between two others, that is two comparisons joined with ∧.

spec.requirement: The six comparisons share one level of precedence and do not associate, and neither do ⊼ and ⊽.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_EXPECTED_EQUALS
diagnostics.message: a type definition is written 'type NAME = ...'
diagnostics.cause: The name of the type is followed by `=` and then by what the type is made of.  There is no form that declares a name without saying what it stands for: a type whose parts are not written is a type nothing can be said about, and the language has no forward declarations because it reads every definition of a file before it checks any of them.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: A type definition is written `type NAME = ...`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_EXPECTED_COLON
diagnostics.message: each part of a type is written 'NAME : TYPE'
diagnostics.cause: A field of a product and a variant of a sum are both written as a name, a colon and a type -- the same shape a parameter and a variable are written with, so that one habit serves for all of them.  A part with no name would be one that could only be reached by counting, and the specification lets the compiler reorder a product's fields, so counting is exactly what it must not be possible to do.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: Each part of a type definition is written `NAME : TYPE`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_MIXED_SEPARATORS
diagnostics.message: this definition separates its parts with {found} after separating them with {first}

args.name: first
args.description: the separator the definition started with

diagnostics.cause: The separator is what says which kind of type is being defined: `;` for a product, which holds all of its parts at once, and `|` for a sum, which holds exactly one of them.  A definition using both would be saying two things about itself, and there is no type that is both.  Which one was meant is what to decide; the first separator is where the definition said so.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: One type definition uses one separator throughout.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_FIRST_SEPARATOR
diagnostics.message: the definition separated its parts with this
diagnostics.cause: Attached to the report of a definition that changed separator part way, pointing at the one it began with.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: One type definition uses one separator throughout.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEDEF_NO_PARTS
diagnostics.message: a type with no parts is 'void' written at greater length
diagnostics.cause: A product of no fields holds nothing, and a sum of no variants has no value at all; `void` is the type of what carries no information, and the language admits one spelling per meaning.  Where a type is wanted that is a name for another type, that is what the to-do list calls an alias and the language does not have yet.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Product and sum types
spec.requirement: A type definition has at least one part.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MATCH_EXPECTED_ARMS
diagnostics.message: the arms of a 'match' follow it, indented or in braces
diagnostics.cause: `match` takes a value apart, so it is written with the value and then the arms that take its alternatives: a colon and an indented run of them, or a braced one.  There is no form with no arms, because a `match` that takes nothing apart does nothing.

spec.requirement: A `match` is written with its arms in one of the two block notations.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_EXPECTED_VALUES
diagnostics.message: the values of an enumeration follow it, indented or in braces
diagnostics.cause: `enum NAME` says what the type is called and nothing about what it holds, so the names of its values follow: a colon and an indented run of them, or a braced one.  Where a type was named as well, the colon that opens the block is a second one -- the first belongs to the type.

spec.requirement: An enumeration is written with its values in one of the two block notations.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_NO_VALUES
diagnostics.message: an enumeration with no values is a type nothing can have
diagnostics.cause: Every value of an enumeration is one of the names its definition lists, so a definition that lists none describes a type no value can be of.  `void` is the type of what carries no information, and is what a program that wants one should say.

spec.requirement: An enumeration has at least one value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ENUMDEF_EXPECTED_VALUE
diagnostics.message: a value of an enumeration is given a number or another of its names, not {found}
diagnostics.cause: `NAME = 4` says which number the value is stored as; `NAME = other` says it is the one `other` already stands for, which is how two names are given one value on purpose.  Nothing else may follow the `=`: an enumeration's values are known while the program is compiled, so there is nothing for an expression to be worked out from.

spec.requirement: A value of an enumeration is given a number or the name of an earlier one.

diagnostics.name: LANG_IF_ELSE_IS_LAST
diagnostics.message: 'else' is the last arm of an 'if'
diagnostics.cause: `else` is the arm that runs when none of the others did, so nothing can be asked after it: an `elif` written there could never be reached, and a second `else` would be a second answer to a question already answered.

spec.requirement: The `else` arm of an `if` is its last.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_CLOSING_SET
diagnostics.message: expected '⸩'
diagnostics.cause: A set, a dictionary and a lookup in either are written between `⸨` and `⸩`, and the closing one is missing here.  What is usually behind it is a comma left out between two entries, or a key written with no value after it.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Sets and dictionaries
spec.requirement: A set, a dictionary and a lookup are closed with `⸩`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_ENTRY_VALUE
diagnostics.message: an entry of a dictionary is written 'KEY : VALUE'
diagnostics.cause: The first entry of this one had a value, so it is a dictionary and every entry of it has one.  A collection whose entries are keys alone is a set, and the two are told apart by the first entry: that is what keeps `⸨a, b⸩` and `⸨a: 1, b: 2⸩` from needing two spellings of the brackets.

spec.section: The Language / Types / Sets and dictionaries
spec.requirement: Every entry of a dictionary written down has a value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ASSIGN_NOT_A_PLACE
diagnostics.message: this is a value, and a value cannot be assigned to
diagnostics.cause: What may stand on the left of `←` is a place: a name, or an entry of a dictionary written the way one is read.  Anything else is a value the program worked out, and there is nowhere for an assignment to put anything.

spec.requirement: The left of an assignment is a name or an entry of a dictionary.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_CLOSING_TUPLE
diagnostics.message: expected '〉'
diagnostics.cause: A tuple and the type of one are written between `〈` and `〉`, and the closing one is missing here.  What is usually behind it is a comma left out between two members.

spec.requirement: A tuple is closed with `〉`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_CLOSING_ARRAY
diagnostics.message: expected '⟧'
diagnostics.cause: An array, the type of one and a lookup in one are all written between `⟦` and `⟧`, and the closing one is missing here.  What is usually behind it is a comma left out between two elements.

spec.requirement: An array is closed with `⟧`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_CLOSING_LIST
diagnostics.message: expected ']'
diagnostics.cause: A list and the type of one are both written between `[` and `]`, and the closing one is missing here.  What is usually behind it is a comma left out between two elements.

spec.requirement: A list is closed with `]`.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_SPREAD_OUTSIDE_A_CALL
diagnostics.message: '⁂' stands among the arguments of a call or the members of a tuple, and nowhere else
diagnostics.cause: The asterism says that several things stand where one is written, which is a thing only a list of things has room for.  An argument list is one and a tuple's members are another; somewhere else exactly one value is wanted, so the glyph would have to mean something else and there is nothing for it to mean -- it is not an expression, and what follows it is not an operand.

spec.requirement: The asterism stands among the arguments of a call.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_EXPECTED_LABEL_NAME
diagnostics.message: expected the name of a loop after '§'
diagnostics.cause: The section sign says that a loop is being named, so a name is what follows it.  Nothing else can: the glyph does nothing on its own.

spec.requirement: A label is written '§' followed by a name.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SYNTAX_JUMP_WITHOUT_A_LABEL
diagnostics.message: '{keyword}' says which loop it means, so a label is written after it
diagnostics.cause: A jump with no label would mean the loop nearest to it, which is a thing that changes when a loop is put around it -- and putting a loop around something is what a program that writes this language does.  Naming the loop makes the jump say what it means rather than where it stands.

spec.requirement: 'break' and 'continue' are each written with the label of the loop they mean.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_UNKNOWN
diagnostics.message: unknown attribute '{name}'
diagnostics.cause: The attribute name is not one the compiler knows.  Attribute names are not an open namespace: an unrecognized name is an error rather than an ignored annotation, so that a misspelling can never silently drop a property the code depends on.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Some functions have to be treated special.  The attribute syntax denotes this status of the function alongside the function definition.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_DUPLICATE
diagnostics.message: attribute '{name}' is applied more than once to the same object
diagnostics.cause: An attribute may appear only once per object.  Where an attribute admits several variants, the variant is selected by a parameter rather than by repeating the attribute.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition / Special Functions
spec.requirement: Some functions have to be treated special.  The attribute syntax denotes this status of the function alongside the function definition.

diagnostics.name: LANG_ATTR_BAD_ARGUMENTS
diagnostics.message: attribute '{name}' {problem}
diagnostics.cause: The arguments do not match the attribute's declared signature.  Attributes take positional arguments first and named arguments after, in the manner of a function call.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LOOP_COMES_TO_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: nothing in this loop gives it a value to come to
diagnostics.cause: Something reads what the loop comes to, and nothing in it produces one: no 'break' hands a value over, and there is no 'else' arm that gives one.  A loop is a statement until something in it says otherwise, which is what a 'break' with a value says.

spec.requirement: A loop whose value is read has a 'break' that hands a value over, or an 'else' arm that gives one.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LOOP_VALUE_MISMATCH
diagnostics.message: '{found}' is given here, and the loop comes to '{expected}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was written

diagnostics.cause: A loop comes to one type, whichever way it was left, so every 'break' in it and its 'else' arm all give that one type -- the block after the loop is reached down all of those ways and reads one thing.  What the type is, is what the loop is being used as where that says, and otherwise what the first thing to give one gave.

spec.requirement: Everything a loop may come to is of one type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CALL_ANSWER_DROPPED
diagnostics.message: nothing takes what '{name}' answers with
diagnostics.cause: A function that answers with something is a function whose answer is the point of calling it, so a call whose answer goes nowhere is either a mistake or a leftover -- and in a language emitted by a generator a leftover is a defect in the generator.  Where the call is meant to be made for what it does and the answer is genuinely not wanted, `_ ← f()` says so in one line; where that is true of every call to the function, `@[can_ignore]` on the function says it once.

spec.requirement: A call whose function answers with something has its answer taken, unless the function is marked '@[can_ignore]'.

diagnostics.name: LANG_WILDCARD_IS_NOT_READ
diagnostics.message: '_' is where a value is put to be dropped, and nothing reads it
diagnostics.cause: '_' is not a variable: it is the place a value is sent to when the program means to work it out and not use it.  Nothing is stored there, so there is nothing to read back.

spec.requirement: '_' may be assigned to and may not be read.

diagnostics.name: LANG_WILDCARD_IS_NOT_DEFINED
diagnostics.message: '_' needs no definition, and having one would make it a name
diagnostics.cause: '_' is where a value is put to be dropped, and it is that everywhere without being defined anywhere.  A definition would make it an ordinary variable in that scope -- one that could be read, and that would have to be 'mut' to be assigned to again -- which is a second meaning for one spelling.

spec.requirement: '_' is not defined.

diagnostics.name: LANG_WILDCARD_TAKES_A_VALUE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' answers with nothing, so there is nothing here to drop
diagnostics.cause: Assigning to '_' says that a value is being worked out and deliberately not used.  Where what is written produces no value there is nothing to say that about, and the call stands on its own as the statement it already is.

spec.requirement: What is assigned to '_' produces a value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PURE_CHANGES_A_VARIABLE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' outlives this call, and a pure function changes nothing that does
diagnostics.cause: A function is pure unless it says otherwise, and what pure means is that calling it changes nothing a later call or a later reader could notice -- which is what lets a caller move a call, make it once instead of twice, or not make it at all.  A variable at the top level exists before the call and after it, so writing one is exactly the thing being ruled out.  Where the change is the point of the function, `@[impure]` on it says so.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: A function without '@[impure]' changes nothing that outlives the call.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PURE_WRITES_ELSEWHERE
diagnostics.message: this writes memory the function did not make, and a pure function does not
diagnostics.cause: A pure function may write its own storage -- an array it made, which is gone when the call ends -- and nothing else.  An array it was handed belongs to the caller, and a set or a dictionary lives in an arena that outlives the call, so writing either is a change someone else can see.  Where that is the point of the function, `@[impure]` on it says so.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: A function without '@[impure]' writes only storage it made itself.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PURE_CALLS_IMPURE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' may change what outlives it, and this function is pure
diagnostics.cause: Whatever the callee may change, the caller may change by calling it, so purity is a property of everything a call reaches and not of one function's own statements.  A function that calls one marked `@[impure]` is therefore marked `@[impure]` itself -- which is the one line that says where the effects in a program begin.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: A function calling one marked '@[impure]' is itself marked '@[impure]'.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LISTABLE_SHAPES_DIFFER
diagnostics.message: this is {found} along, and another being walked is {wanted}

args.name: found
args.description: how many this argument has along the dimension being walked

diagnostics.cause: Two things walked together are walked in step: the first of one goes with the first of the other, and there is no first of one to go with a second the other does not have.  One that is not an array is not walked at all and is used at every turn, so the rule is about the ones being walked and about nothing else.  It is the same rule for an operator's two sides as for a listable function's arguments.

spec.requirement: Arguments walked together have the same number along the dimension being walked.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LISTABLE_CANNOT_WALK
diagnostics.message: '{found}' cannot be walked down to the '{wanted}' that is wanted here

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was handed over

args.name: wanted
args.description: the type wanted -- a parameter's, or what an operator is defined on

diagnostics.cause: Walking takes one dimension off an array at a time and stops when what is left is what is wanted: what a parameter takes, or what an operator is defined on.  Where the two never meet -- an array of a different element type, or one of a length the type does not say, whose shape the answer would have to be and is not known -- there is no walk to make.

spec.requirement: Anything walked has a type the walk reaches the wanted one from, and every dimension walked is one the type states.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LISTABLE_TAKES_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: '{name}' takes no arguments, so there is nothing for it to be walked over
diagnostics.cause: What the attribute says is what happens when an array is handed where one element is wanted.  A function that takes nothing is a function nothing can be handed to, so the attribute says nothing about it and is more likely a mistake than a thing that was meant.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: A function marked '@[listable]' takes at least one argument.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MASK_WRONG_SHAPE
diagnostics.message: a mask of '{found}' does not pick out of '{wanted}'

args.name: wanted
args.description: the type of the array being picked from

diagnostics.cause: A mask says, of each thing it could pick, whether to pick it -- so it has one truth value for each, and its shape is the array's first dimensions, as many of them as it has.  A mask of one dimension over a table picks rows; a mask of two picks elements.  A shape that is neither leaves things it says nothing about, or says something about things that are not there.

spec.requirement: A mask's shape is the leading dimensions of the array it picks from.

diagnostics.name: LANG_MASK_NEEDS_A_STATED_SHAPE
diagnostics.message: picking out of '{found}' needs a shape the type states

args.name: found
args.description: the type of the array being picked from

diagnostics.cause: What picking answers with is however many were picked, held in room enough for all of them -- and room enough for all of them is what the shape says.  Where the type does not say it, the room would have to be taken while the program runs, which is an allocation and a change to something that outlives the call.

spec.requirement: An array picked from states its shape.

diagnostics.name: LANG_WRAP_TAKES_ONE_EXPRESSION
diagnostics.message: '⎕wrap' is written around one expression, and {found} were given

args.name: found
args.description: how many expressions were written inside it

diagnostics.cause: '⎕wrap' is not a function and takes no arguments: it is written around the one expression whose operators are to go past the ends of their types rather than stopping the program.  Written around none or around several there is no such expression.

spec.requirement: '⎕wrap' is written around exactly one expression.

diagnostics.name: LANG_WRAP_SATURATING_INSIDE
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' stops at the end of its type, and '⎕wrap' says the operators inside it do not

args.name: operator
args.description: the saturating operator that was written

diagnostics.cause: A wrap says one thing about every operator written inside it: that going past the end of the type is what was meant and the low bits are the answer.  A saturating operator says the opposite about itself, that the end of the type is the answer.  Only one of the two can be what the program meant, and which one is not something to guess at.  Where the saturating step really was meant, it is written outside the wrap and its answer handed in.

spec.requirement: The saturating operators are not written inside '⎕wrap'.

diagnostics.name: LANG_WRAP_IS_NOT_A_VALUE
diagnostics.message: '⎕wrap' is not a value; it is written around the expression whose operators are to wrap
diagnostics.cause: '⎕wrap' looks like a function and is not one.  There is nothing for it to stand for on its own: what it does is decide what the operators written inside it mean, which is a property of where they are written and not a value that can be passed about.

spec.requirement: '⎕wrap' appears only with an expression written inside it.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CONCAT_NEEDS_AN_ARRAY
diagnostics.message: '⧺' joins two arrays, and '{found}' is not one

args.name: found
args.description: the type of the side that is not an array

diagnostics.cause: Joining puts the elements of one array after the elements of another, which is a thing to do to arrays and to nothing else.  A single value is made an array of one by writing it between the array brackets.

spec.requirement: Both sides of '⧺' are arrays.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CONCAT_NEEDS_A_STATED_SHAPE
diagnostics.message: joining '{found}' needs a shape the type states

args.name: found
args.description: the type of the side whose shape the type does not state

diagnostics.cause: What a join answers with is as long as its two sides together, and room for that many has to be taken where the join stands.  Where the type does not say how long a side is, how much room to take is not known until the program runs, which is an allocation and a change to something that outlives the call.

spec.requirement: Both sides of '⧺' state their shape.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CONCAT_ELEMENTS_DIFFER
diagnostics.message: '{left}' and '{right}' hold different things, and a join holds one

args.name: left
args.description: the type of the left side

args.name: right
args.description: the type of the right side

diagnostics.cause: An array holds values of one type, so an array made out of two others holds what both of them held.  Where the two held different things there is no such type, and which of the two the answer would be is not something to guess at.

spec.requirement: The two sides of '⧺' are arrays of one element type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CONCAT_SHAPES_DIFFER
diagnostics.message: '{left}' and '{right}' differ in a dimension other than the first

args.name: left
args.description: the type of the left side

args.name: right
args.description: the type of the right side

diagnostics.cause: A join puts rows after rows, which is the first dimension growing and every dimension inside it staying as it was: two tables of three columns each join into a table of three columns.  Where the inner dimensions differ there are no rows of one shape to put after one another, and neither is a two-dimensional array joined to a one-dimensional one.

spec.requirement: The two sides of '⧺' agree about every dimension but the first.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CHAR_OUTSIDE_UNICODE
diagnostics.message: {value} is not a code point; the last one is U+{last}

args.name: last
args.description: the last code point there is, in hexadecimal

diagnostics.cause: A value of 'char' is a Unicode code point, and there is a last one: U+10FFFF, which is as far as UTF-16's surrogate pairs reach and which every encoding has had to agree with since.  A number above it, or below zero, is not a code point at all -- and 'char' being held in thirty-two bits says how much room one takes, not which numbers are values of it.

spec.requirement: A value of 'char' is between U+0000 and U+10FFFF.

diagnostics.name: LANG_CHAR_TAKES_ONE
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is written around one expression, and {found} were given

args.name: name
args.description: which of the two was written

args.name: found
args.description: how many expressions were written inside it

diagnostics.cause: Each of the two takes exactly one value: '⎕ord' the code point whose number is wanted, and '⎕chr' the number whose code point is wanted.  Neither has a reading for none or for several.

spec.requirement: 'ord' and 'chr' each take one value.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LENGTH_HAS_NO_COUNT
diagnostics.message: '#' asks how many, and '{found}' is not made of a number of things

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was asked

diagnostics.cause: '#' answers how many things something is made of: the characters of a string, the outermost dimension of an array, the members of a tuple, what a set or a dictionary holds.  A value that is one thing is not made of a number of things, and answering one for it would be answering a question nobody asked.

spec.requirement: '#' is written before a string, an array, a tuple, a set or a dictionary.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SHAPE_NOT_WRITTEN_DOWN
diagnostics.message: the shape on the left of '⍴' has to be written down
diagnostics.cause: An array carries its shape in its type, so how many there are along each dimension is settled while the program is compiled and not while it runs.  A shape worked out from something the compiler cannot see would be a shape the type could not say, which is an array whose room is taken while the program runs -- an allocation, and a different thing from this.

spec.requirement: The shape on the left of '⍴' is a number, or a tuple of numbers, known while compiling.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SHAPE_NOT_A_COUNT
diagnostics.message: {found} is not a length; a shape says how many, which is more than none
diagnostics.cause: Each number of a shape says how many there are along one dimension.  None of them is a length: an array with no elements along a dimension has no elements at all, and this language has no such array.  Neither is a negative number, there being no such count.

spec.requirement: Every number of a shape is greater than zero.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SHAPE_TOO_MANY
diagnostics.message: {found} values will not fit a shape that holds {wanted}

args.name: wanted
args.description: how many the new object holds

diagnostics.cause: The values on the right of the operator fill the new object, going round again where there are fewer of them than it holds.  More of them than it holds is the other way round, and there is no reading of it: which ones would be left out is not something to guess at, and a program that meant to leave some out can say which.

spec.requirement: The right of the operator has no more elements than the shape on the left holds.

diagnostics.name: LANG_SHAPE_HAS_NONE
diagnostics.message: '⍴' answers a shape, and '{found}' has none

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was asked

diagnostics.cause: A shape is how many there are along each dimension, which is a thing an array has and other things do not.  What a string, a tuple, a set or a dictionary is made of is one number rather than a shape, and '#' is what asks for it.

spec.requirement: '⍴' written before one thing is written before an array.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LIST_ELEMENTS_DIFFER
diagnostics.message: a list holds one type for now, and '{found}' is not '{wanted}'

args.name: found
args.description: the type of the element that does not agree

args.name: wanted
args.description: the type the list turned out to hold

diagnostics.cause: A list is the sequence whose elements need not be of one type.  What makes that work is boxing -- a value held with enough beside it to say what it is -- which this compiler does not do yet, so for now they must agree.  The type a list holds is recorded so that when boxing arrives, the case where they do agree is the one worth not boxing and is still there to be found.

spec.requirement: Every element of a list is of one type, until boxing.

diagnostics.name: LANG_LIST_HOLDS_NOTHING
diagnostics.message: a list written with nothing in it does not say what it holds
diagnostics.cause: A list carries the type of what it holds, and one with nothing in it has nothing to say it with.  Where such a list stands somewhere that wants a particular one -- the value of a name whose type is written, an argument, what a function answers with -- that is what it holds; where nothing wants one, there is nothing to take it from.

spec.requirement: A list with nothing in it takes the type wanted where it stands.

diagnostics.name: LANG_COMPTIME_NOT_SETTLED
diagnostics.message: this is not a question the compiler can settle
diagnostics.cause: A condition written after 'comptime' is answered while the program is compiled, so it may only ask what the compiler knows: whether two types are the one type, written with '⎕typeof' and a type's name, and those joined with the logical operators.  Anything about a value is a question about what the program does, which is what an ordinary condition is for.

spec.requirement: A condition after 'comptime' asks only about types.

diagnostics.name: LANG_COMPTIME_NEEDS_A_TUPLE
diagnostics.message: a loop settled while compiling takes its turns from a tuple, and '{found}' is not one

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what the loop was given

diagnostics.cause: A 'comptime foreach' is written out, one body per turn, which is what lets each turn's value be of a different type.  A tuple is the only thing whose values are of types written one by one; everything else holds values of one type, and a loop over one of those is an ordinary loop.

spec.requirement: A 'comptime foreach' takes its turns from a tuple.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FOREACH_TUPLE_NEEDS_COMPTIME
diagnostics.message: a tuple's members are of the types they were written with, so a loop over one is written 'comptime foreach'
diagnostics.cause: Every turn of an ordinary loop binds a name of one type, because the loop is one body run again.  A tuple's members are of whatever types they were written with, so a loop over one has to be written out -- one body per member, each with its own type -- which is what 'comptime' says.

spec.requirement: A loop over a tuple is written 'comptime foreach'.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPEOF_OUTSIDE_COMPTIME
diagnostics.message: '⎕typeof' stands in a condition settled while compiling and nowhere else
diagnostics.cause: What '⎕typeof' answers is a type, and a type is not a value: there is nothing for one to be at run time, which is why the representation is deliberately unspecified.  Where it may stand is the one place the answer is wanted and never has to exist -- a condition the compiler settles.

spec.requirement: '⎕typeof' appears only in a condition after 'comptime'.

diagnostics.name: LANG_EXTREMUM_HAS_NONE
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' answers the largest or smallest of several, and '{found}' is not several of one ordered thing

args.name: operator
args.description: which of the two was written

args.name: found
args.description: the type of what was asked

diagnostics.cause: Written before one thing, these answer the largest or the smallest of what it holds -- the elements of an array or a list, the keys of a set or a dictionary, the characters of a string, the members of a tuple.  What they hold has to be something a comparison orders, which is a number or a code point; and a tuple's members have to be of one type, there being no comparing two things of two types.

spec.section: The Language / Expressions / Largest and smallest
spec.requirement: '⌈' and '⌊' written before one thing are written before several values of one ordered type.

diagnostics.name: LANG_TYPE_OPERAND_NOT_FLOAT
diagnostics.message: '{operator}' rounds floating-point numbers, not '{found}'
diagnostics.cause: The four roundings answer the whole number a floating-point number rounds to, in the type it was given.  An integer is already a whole number, so rounding one would answer with what it was handed; a value of any other type is not a number and has nothing to round.

spec.requirement: The four rounding operators are defined on floating-point values only.

diagnostics.name: LANG_PURE_READS_THE_ROUNDING_MODE
diagnostics.message: '⇕' rounds by the processor's own rounding mode, and a pure function does not read it
diagnostics.cause: Three of the four roundings say which way they go, and two of one with the same value answer alike wherever the program runs.  The fourth asks the processor what it is doing just now, which is state outside the function and outside the language, so a function that writes it can answer differently in two places for the same argument -- which is the one thing a pure function promises not to do.  Where reading the mode is the point, `@[impure]` on the function says so; where it is not, one of the other three says which way to go.

spec.requirement: A function writing '⇕' is marked '@[impure]'.

diagnostics.name: LANG_STMT_UNREACHABLE
diagnostics.message: statements after this one are never executed
diagnostics.cause: The statement before this one leaves the block it stands in -- 'return' leaves the function, 'break' leaves a loop, 'continue' begins the loop's next turn -- so nothing after it in that block can run.  This is usually leftover code, or a jump that was meant to be conditional.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Function return values are specified with the `return` keyword.  The function immediately returns and the remaining statements in the block are ignored (the compiler must issue a warning in this case).  If the `return` statement is the last statement in the function then the `return` keywords can and should be skipped (a warning is issued in this case).

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_REDUNDANT
diagnostics.message: 'return' can and should be omitted on the last statement of a function
diagnostics.cause: When the value of the last statement is the function's result, the 'return' keyword carries no information and is omitted in the canonical form of the language.  The compiler's own output never writes it.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Function return values are specified with the `return` keyword.  The function immediately returns and the remaining statements in the block are ignored (the compiler must issue a warning in this case).  If the `return` statement is the last statement in the function then the `return` keywords can and should be skipped (a warning is issued in this case).

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_MISSING
diagnostics.message: control reaches the end of '{name}' without producing a value of type '{type}'
diagnostics.cause: A function whose return type is not 'void' must produce a value on every path that leaves it.  Because the language admits no undefined behaviour, falling off the end is an error rather than an unspecified result.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: the code behaves, when executed, exactly as the code describes it. No undefined behavior, no surprising interpretation of inputs.

diagnostics.name: LANG_FUNCDEF_RETURN_VALUE_IN_VOID
diagnostics.message: returning a value from '{name}', which is declared to return 'void'
diagnostics.cause: The function declares no result, so there is nothing for the returned value to become.

spec.section: The Language / File Structure / Function Definition
spec.requirement: Function return values are specified with the `return` keyword.  The function immediately returns and the remaining statements in the block are ignored (the compiler must issue a warning in this case).  If the `return` statement is the last statement in the function then the `return` keywords can and should be skipped (a warning is issued in this case).

diagnostics.name: LANG_STMT_VALUE_DISCARDED
diagnostics.message: the value of this statement is not used
diagnostics.cause: An expression computes a value and does nothing else, so a statement that is nothing but an expression is a statement with no effect unless something takes the value.  Something does take it in exactly one place: the last statement of a body is the body's result.  Everywhere else the value goes nowhere, and a line that goes nowhere is either a mistake or a leftover -- a generator that emits one has a defect, which is the reason this is an error rather than a warning.  Where the line is meant to stand as it is, `@[ignore(5005)]` on the statement says so.

spec.section: The Language / Expressions / Statements that are expressions
spec.requirement: A statement that is an expression must have its value used; the last statement of a body is the body's result.

diagnostics.name: LANG_STMT_ASSIGNMENT_IS_AN_ARROW
diagnostics.message: '=' compares two values; an assignment is written '←'
diagnostics.cause: Attached where the discarded value is a comparison written with '=', which is what someone writes who has spent years in a language where '=' assigns.  The diagnostic itself says the value goes nowhere; this says why the line was probably written.

spec.requirement: An assignment is written `NAME ← VALUE`.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_BACKEND_UNSUPPORTED
diagnostics.message: the bootstrap compiler cannot generate code for {construct} yet

args.name: construct
args.description: the construct that has no code generation yet

diagnostics.cause: The bootstrap compiler implements only as much of the language as the compiler's own source needs, so a construct the specification describes may still have no code generation.  This is a limitation of the bootstrap compiler and not an error in the program; the same program will compile once the construct is implemented.

spec.requirement: It does not have to be able to handle the entire language as per the specification as long as it can compile the code of the actual compiler.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_BACKEND_NEEDS_AN_EXTENSION
diagnostics.message: this needs the {extension} extension, and the program is built for '{level}', which has not got it

args.name: extension
args.description: what the code generator would have needed

args.name: level
args.description: what the program was asked to be built for

diagnostics.cause: On an architecture whose base is small and whose every capability is an extension, what a program may use is what it was built for.  Where it uses something the extensions do not cover, the answer is not to emit it anyway -- that is a program that does not run -- and not to emulate it either, since an emulation of a floating-point convention is a different calling convention and a different ABI.  So it is refused, and the two ways out are to build for something that has the extension, with '--mclevel', or to write the program without whatever wanted it.

spec.requirement: A program uses only what the ISA it is built for provides.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_BACKEND_UNENCODABLE
diagnostics.message: instruction cannot be encoded: {detail}
diagnostics.cause: The instruction, its operands, or the combination of the two cannot be represented in the target's encoding.  From generated code this reports a defect in the compiler; once inline assembly exists it will also report a constraint the written instruction violates, such as naming a high-byte register in a form that carries a REX prefix.

spec.requirement: The backends should use a symbolic version to generate the assembler code to allow, in future, inline assembler code.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_IMAGE_UNDEFINED_SYMBOL
diagnostics.message: '{name}' is referenced but never defined
diagnostics.cause: Compilation covers the whole program at once and there is no equivalent of an object file, so every symbol the generated code refers to must be defined by the same compilation.  A symbol that is still undefined at image generation means a function the program calls was never given a body.

spec.requirement: At least for the time being there is only whole-program compilation.  There is no equivalent of object files.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_IMAGE_VALUE_OUT_OF_RANGE
diagnostics.message: a value of {value} does not fit the {field} field that must hold it

args.name: value
args.description: the value that does not fit

diagnostics.cause: A displacement, an address or an initial value has to fit the field the instruction or the image reserves for it.  One that does not is reported rather than stored with its upper bits dropped: a program that branched to an address other than the one it named, or started with a value other than the one it was given, would be behaving otherwise than it reads.  A branch too far to reach is the usual cause, and needs a longer form of the instruction, which this compiler does not choose yet.  That a value fits where it is stored is one of the checks the compiler always performs, rather than one it leaves to the reader to have made.

spec.requirement: The compiler predominently has to be fast while at the same time always perform all conformance checks and generating small code.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_INTERNAL_ERROR
diagnostics.message: internal compiler error: {detail}
diagnostics.cause: The compiler detected an inconsistency in its own data structures, which always indicates a defect in the compiler rather than in the compiled program.  Please report it together with the source that triggered it.

diagnostics.name: IMPL_UNIMPLEMENTED_FEATURE
diagnostics.message: {feature} is not implemented yet

args.name: feature
args.description: the feature the specification describes but the compiler lacks

diagnostics.cause: The specification describes this, and the compiler does not implement it yet.  It reports a gap in the compiler rather than a defect in the program: the same program will compile once the feature exists.

spec.requirement: It does not have to be able to handle the entire language as per the specification as long as it can compile the code of the actual compiler.
